The morning light hit the windowsill differently that Tuesday, slanting through dust motes that seemed suspended in some private conspiracy of physics. I had been thinking about my grandmother's hands, the way her knuckles swelled like tiny walnuts in her final years, how she still peeled apples with surgical precision, the red ribbon of skin falling in one continuous spiral.

Memory is not a file cabinet. It's more like a garden where things grow unexpected, where the tomato you planted in May becomes something else entirely by August, where the soil remembers floods you have forgotten. I read once that every time you recall something, you alter it slightly, like a Chinese whisper with yourself. This terrifies me and comforts me in equal measure. It means my worst days are editable. It means my best days are probably half-fabricated already.

I knew a man in Portland who kept pigeons on his roof. Not fancy breeds, just the ordinary gray kind you see in every parking lot, the ones we call flying rats. He named them all after jazz musicians. Miles would land on his shoulder and peck at his earlobe. Coltrane refused to enter the coop at night and slept on the antenna, winter and summer both. He told me pigeons can find their way home from hundreds of miles away using magnetic fields and smell, a combination of the cosmic and the mundane that seems almost too perfect, too metaphorically convenient. I didn't believe him about the names until he called out and they came, one by one, settling on the tar paper in a row like notes on a staff.

We are all of us navigating by invisible fields. The pull of childhood kitchens. The scent of someone who left. I cannot pass a certain intersection in Chicago without feeling the ghost weight of a backpack I carried at twenty-two, the specific ache of walking twelve blocks because I couldn't afford the bus, the pride and the poverty braided together so tight I still can't separate them. The brain stores emotion in the amygdala but the story of the emotion in the hippocampus, and when trauma disrupts this collaboration, you end up with fear that has no narrative, panic attacks triggered by nothing you can name. I think about this when I wake at 3 AM with my heart racing and no enemy in sight.

My friend Elena makes pottery and talks about the moment of centering, when the clay finds the middle of the wheel and suddenly everything is possible. Before that, she says, it's just fighting. The clay wins, you win, nobody wins. But centering is not something you force. You have to stop trying so hard. The clay teaches you this by failing, over and over, collapsing into wobble, becoming something you didn't plan. The best pieces, she told me, come from the salvage, the collapse that revealed something you couldn't have designed.

I have been trying to center for forty years.

The last time I saw my father, we talked about nothing important. The weather. A restaurant renovation downtown. I didn't know it was the last time. This is the banality the movies never prepare you for, how ordinary the final ordinary moments are, how you would have paid everything you own for one more conversation about nothing, one more chance to not say anything significant, to just be in the room with the person while the light did whatever it was doing, while dust motes performed their invisible choreography.

There is a word in Japanese, *aware*, for the bittersweetness of things passing. Not nostalgia, which is too self-conscious, too curated. *Aware* is the sharpness of cherry blossoms because they fall, the price of beauty being its temporary nature. The Japanese language has other words I wish English had: *kintsugi*, the art of repairing broken pottery with gold, making the damage visible and valuable; *komorebi*, sunlight filtering through leaves; *tsundoku*, the act of acquiring books and letting them pile up unread. We need more words for the specific loneliness of unread books, the promise deferred, the self we imagined we would become.

I have three hundred books I haven't read. I keep buying more. This is either hope or delusion, and I no longer know the difference.

The pigeon man died last spring. His daughter, who had never understood the birds, opened the coop and let them go. They circled the building for three days, she told me, before they finally dispersed. Miles was the last to leave. She recognized him by the white patch on his left wing, the one her father had described at the funeral, crying in a way that surprised everyone, this rough man in his sixties weeping for a pigeon named after a trumpet player dead before he was born.

I don't know what happened to Miles. Whether he found another roof, another hand. Whether he lived out whatever span pigeons live, three years, five, more if they're lucky and avoid the hawks and the poison and the children with rocks. I don't know if pigeons feel the equivalent of *aware*, if the magnetic field they follow home eventually becomes just habit, just the only thing they know to do, or if each return carries some version of relief, of rightness, of the center holding.

The morning light is different now. It's afternoon, the slant gone vertical, the dust motes invisible in the brightness. I have used most of my words and said almost nothing I planned. This is the salvage, the collapse, the something I couldn't design. The clay is still wet. The wheel still turns.
